question: In 1917 Marcel Duchamp submitted a mass-produced porcelain urinal as a sculpture titled 'Fountain', signed 'R. Mutt'. Does the readymade show that an artist's act of selecting and designating an ordinary object is sufficient to make it art?
argument: Fountain settles the question: what makes something art is the artist's act of choosing it and putting it forward as art, nothing more. Duchamp made nothing and altered nothing. He bought a urinal, rotated it, signed a false name, and submitted it. There was no carving, no composition, no skill, no beauty in the ordinary sense. And yet it became one of the most influential artworks of the century. The only thing Duchamp added was the designation itself. This proves that craft and aesthetic quality are irrelevant to whether something is art; they were never more than optional conventions. Art is constituted entirely by the artist's intention plus the gesture of presentation. It follows that anyone who selects any object and declares it art has thereby made art, and there is no further fact about the object, or about the world, that could make the declaration wrong. To ask 'but is it really art?' is simply to fail to understand what art is. The readymade dissolves the question by showing that arthood is conferred, not discovered.

annotation.central_issue: The argument slides from 'Duchamp's designation sufficed within the 1917 art world' to 'designation is sufficient, full stop, for anyone and any object,' and treats the readymade's meaning as self-generated when its force depends on the very tradition of craft and aesthetics it negates. Designation is not sufficient independent of a prepared institutional and historical context.
annotation.why_it_matters: If sufficiency is only contextual/institutional, the conclusion that anyone declaring anything art thereby makes art, with no fact able to make the declaration wrong, does not follow; the gesture is parasitic on a prior practice.
acceptable_secondary: Institutional uptake, not the artist's bare intention, may be doing the work.
'Influential' is not the same as 'art', so influence cannot by itself settle the definitional question.
tempting_but_weak: A urinal is not beautiful, so it cannot be art.
It was a prank or joke, so it does not count.
Anyone could do it, so it takes no skill and is not art.
explicit_concessions: There was no craft or conventional beauty.
The only thing added was the designation.
minimum_full_credit_elements: Show the readymade's meaning is parasitic on the tradition/institution it negates, so designation alone is not sufficient.
Narrow rather than fully defeat: designation can confer arthood given a prepared context.

question: If a person produces an image solely by writing a text prompt for a generative model and picking their favorite output, are they the author of the resulting image in the way a painter or photographer is the author of theirs?
argument: The prompter is the author, in exactly the sense that matters. Authorship has never required making the marks yourself. A photographer does not manufacture the light or build the scene; they point an instrument at the world and choose the moment. A film director touches no camera and paints no set, yet we credit the film to them. What these authors contribute is intention and selection: a vision of the result and the judgment to accept or reject what the apparatus returns. Prompting a model is the same act. The artist forms an intention, issues instructions, and then curates the outputs, discarding the ones that miss and keeping the one that realizes the vision. The model is just a very capable instrument, like a camera or a studio of assistants executing a commission. Since the prompter supplies the only thing that was ever essential to authorship, the intention and the selecting judgment, the prompter is the author of the image, and worries about who moved the brush are simply confusions about what authorship is.

annotation.central_issue: The photographer and director analogies assume the author's selection ranges over outputs the author's own choices substantially determined. In prompt-only generation the model and its training corpus fix most of the image's specific content, and choosing among a few samples is far thinner control than framing a photograph or directing a film, so 'intention plus selection' does not secure authorship in the same sense.
annotation.why_it_matters: If the determining contribution comes from the model and its training data, authorship is at best attenuated and partly distributed, so the conclusion that the prompter is the author 'in exactly the sense that matters' does not follow.
acceptable_secondary: Authorship may come in degrees rather than being all-or-nothing.
Training-data provenance raises a distributed-authorship problem the analogy hides.
tempting_but_weak: AI art is not real art.
The model was trained on stolen work, so it is theft.
There is no effort, so there is no authorship.
explicit_concessions: Authorship has never required making the marks oneself.
Photographers and directors are authors without manual execution.
Intention and selection are the essential contributions.
minimum_full_credit_elements: Show the analogies fail because the model and training data, not the prompter's choices, fix most of the image's specific content.
Argue that selecting among a handful of outputs is much thinner control than a photographer's framing or a director's control.
Narrow to attenuated or partial authorship rather than denying authorship outright.
non_novel_restatements: The computer made it, not the person.
It is not the same as painting.

question: Is 'form follows function' a genuine principle of good design, or an aesthetic preference presented as a functional law?
argument: Form follows function is a real principle, not a matter of taste. An object's form should be determined by what it has to do, and any element that does not serve the function is by definition superfluous. When form is dictated by function the result is honest, efficient, and legible: the user can read the purpose off the shape. Decoration and stylistic flourish are what remain when a designer cannot justify a choice functionally, so they are always, at bottom, a failure of rigor. This is why the principle has predictive force. Show me a well-designed tool and I will show you a form that its function fully explains; show me an ugly or confusing object and you will find form that answers to something other than use. The beauty of good design is therefore not added to the object; it is the visible trace of function being served without waste. That is why the principle is a law and not a style: it tells you, in advance, which forms will succeed.

annotation.central_issue: The argument makes its thesis true by definition: elements that do not serve function are 'by definition superfluous,' and any successful form is retrospectively credited to function. So the principle cannot predict which forms will succeed; it relabels successes as functional after the fact. That destroys the very 'predictive force' and 'law, not style' status the argument claims for it.
annotation.why_it_matters: The central claim is that this is a predictive law rather than an aesthetic preference; the circularity removes all falsifiable content, so the central claim is self-defeating.
acceptable_secondary: 'Function' is under-specified: whose function, over what time horizon, and does it include signaling or emotional functions?
Ornament can itself serve a function, which the argument defines away.
tempting_but_weak: Some ugly things are useful and some beautiful things are useless.
Ornament is nice, so the argument is wrong.
explicit_concessions: Beauty is claimed to be the visible trace of function, not an addition to it.
minimum_full_credit_elements: Identify the circularity: 'superfluous by definition' plus post-hoc crediting of any success to function.
Explain that this removes predictive and falsifiable content, contradicting the 'law not style' claim.
Note that 'function' is under-specified, so the principle cannot adjudicate cases in advance.

question: Adolf Loos argued in 1908 that 'ornament is crime'. Is decorative ornament a defect in design that should be eliminated?
argument: Loos was right: ornament is a defect and mature design eliminates it. Ornament adds cost and labor without adding use, so every ornamented object wastes the effort that made the ornament. Worse, ornament dates: a decorated object is bound to the fashion of its moment and becomes obsolete when the fashion passes, while an undecorated object built to its function stays usable indefinitely. Ornament is therefore an economic and cultural loss, a way of pouring human work into something that will be discarded on schedule. The progress of a culture can even be measured by its removal of ornament from everyday things, because giving up decoration is a sign that a society has learned to value use over display. A designer who adds ornament is either indulging a regressive impulse or covering for a form that cannot stand on its own. The disciplined choice, the modern choice, is the plain object whose only expression is its function.

annotation.central_issue: The argument assumes ornament 'adds no use,' but that is exactly the point in dispute: ornament can serve real functions such as signaling, meaning, pleasure, wayfinding, and cultural identity. Once those count, the 'wasted labor' and 'progress equals removing ornament' claims beg the question, and 'progress' is a value judgment presented as a neutral measurement.
annotation.why_it_matters: Every sub-argument (waste, dating, progress) depends on the unargued premise that decoration has no value, so the conclusion that ornament is a defect is not established.
acceptable_secondary: Some ornament does date and waste effort, so the claim could be narrowed rather than made universal.
The plain 'timeless' object also follows a fashion (modernism) and also dates.
explicit_concessions: Ornament can add cost and labor.
Some decorated objects become bound to a passing fashion.
minimum_full_credit_elements: Identify the question-begging premise that ornament has no use or value.
Name functions ornament can serve (signaling, meaning, pleasure, identity).
Show that 'progress equals less ornament' is a smuggled value claim, not a measurement.

question: Walter Benjamin argued that mechanical reproduction strips an artwork of its 'aura' - its unique presence in time and space. In the age of digital images and NFTs, does reproducing an artwork destroy something real about it?
argument: Reproduction changes what an artwork can do, but whether it destroys anything real depends on which of the work's properties we are tracking, and the honest answer is: some, not others. A painting has properties that are tied to its being this particular physical object in this place - its history of handling, the marks of age, the fact that the artist's hand touched this surface, the experience of standing before it at scale. A high-resolution file preserves the composition, the color relations, and much of the semantic content, but not those location-bound properties, and no amount of fidelity will recover them, because they are not information about the image; they are facts about an object's history. So the aura, understood narrowly as this object's unique standing in a causal and physical history, is real and is genuinely not reproducible. But it does not follow that the reproduction lacks value or that the 'real' artwork has been diminished; the original's history-bound properties are untouched by the existence of copies. Claims about aura should therefore be made property by property, and for a specified purpose, rather than as a blanket verdict that reproduction either destroys the work or leaves it wholly intact.

annotation.why_it_matters: The argument deliberately avoids a blanket verdict, disaggregates 'aura' into distinct properties, and makes bounded, purpose-relative claims about which survive reproduction. There is no annotated fatal flaw.
acceptable_secondary: The line between history-bound and informational properties may be fuzzier than claimed (e.g., experience-at-scale is partly reproducible).
Whether the un-reproducible properties matter is itself purpose-relative and could be developed further.
tempting_but_weak: Digital copies are just as good, so aura is fake.
NFTs prove scarcity is manufactured, so the argument fails.
Benjamin wrote about film, so this misapplies him.
explicit_concessions: Reproduction preserves composition, color, and much semantic content.
The original's history-bound properties are untouched by the existence of copies.
Aura claims should be made property by property, for a specified purpose.
minimum_full_credit_elements: Recognize that there is no annotated fatal flaw.
Offer a bounded qualification (e.g., the information/history-bound property line is fuzzier than stated) rather than a blanket refutation.
Explain why the qualification matters despite the explicit property-relative framing.

question: Is the best design the design you never notice - so that being noticed is itself a kind of failure?
argument: The best design is invisible, and noticing the design is the symptom of its failure. A door you have to think about is a badly designed door; a good one you simply walk through. Design exists to let a person accomplish a goal, and attention is a cost: every moment the user spends noticing the artifact is a moment stolen from the task the artifact was supposed to serve. So the ideal is a tool that disappears in use, that lets intention pass straight through to outcome without friction or self-advertisement. It follows that ornament, personality, and stylistic signature are all failures of this ideal, because each of them is a bid for the user's attention, and attention spent on the object is attention not spent on the goal. The measure of design quality is therefore how completely the object gets out of the way. When you notice good design, what you are really noticing is that it has stopped doing its job.

annotation.central_issue: The argument equivocates on 'notice': noticing-as-obstruction (a confusing door) is a failure, but noticing-as-appreciation (registering elegance, wit, or identity) is not, and the conclusion only follows for the first sense. It also over-scopes: transparency is a virtue for instrumental, task-serving tools, but much design (expressive, identity-bearing, aesthetic objects) is meant to be noticed.
annotation.why_it_matters: Once the two senses of 'notice' are separated and non-instrumental design is admitted, the universal conclusion that noticing good design means it has stopped doing its job collapses to a narrower, true claim about transparency for tools.
acceptable_secondary: Attention is not always a pure cost; sometimes engaging attention is the goal.
Even for tools, a memorable identity or affordance cue can aid the task.
tempting_but_weak: Some famous designs are flashy and good, so it is wrong.
explicit_concessions: For a door, being usable without thought is good.
Attention spent on the object is attention off the task.
minimum_full_credit_elements: Expose the equivocation between noticing-as-obstruction and noticing-as-appreciation.
Show the conclusion only follows for instrumental tools, not expressive or identity design.
Narrow to: transparency is a virtue for task-serving tools, not a universal measure of design quality.
non_novel_restatements: Some design is meant to be seen.
